I have farmed these lands in Quzhou County for nearly fifty years. I am sixty-five now, and my back is not strong like before, but I still know every corner of my five mu of flat land on the North China Plain. I only went to primary school, but farming is what I understand best. My husband passed away years ago, and my son works in the county town, so he can only come back to help with machine work during busy times. I make the decisions myself, and I do not try fancy new things.

The wheat is already in the ground — I planted it last October after rotary tilling the soil and sowing about thirty jin of improved wheat seed per mu. Now it is spring, and I must take care of it until harvest in June. I will topdress with urea once more when the weather warms, and I will irrigate three more times: at green-up, jointing, and grain-filling. I also need to spray four times — herbicide once for the weeds, insecticide twice for aphids, and fungicide once to stop rust. If the weather is fair, I expect around 1000 jin per mu.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I will plant summer maize immediately on the same five mu. I will buy hybrid seed from the shop — probably Denghai 605 or something similar that the neighbors use. I will not till the soil; I will direct-seed into the wheat stubble to save time and fuel, and because my son says no-tillage is good for the soil. I will put down compound fertilizer at planting, irrigate twice during the summer, and spray insecticide twice and herbicide once. I hope to get about 1150 jin per mu.

I do not grow cotton or those special crops like stevia. I am too old for the extra labor of pruning and spraying every week, and the market for those is risky. Wheat and maize are safe. The grain buyers always come to our village, and we can sell easily. I also keep some flour and grain for my own food. This is the rotation my parents taught me, and it has always fed my family. At my age, I stick with what I know.
